t: #3537 Maximum Sum of Edge Values in a Graph — Zigzag Value Assignment
o: With degree ≤ 2 and connectivity, the graph is a disjoint set of paths and cycles (m = n ⇒ all cycles, m = n−1 ⇒ one path). Larger components should receive larger values since edge products grow multiplicatively, and a cycle (one extra edge) outranks a path of equal size. Within a component, the optimal layout interleaves small and large values so the biggest numbers sit adjacent: for a path, values sorted ascending arranged as v0, v2, v4, …, then the odd indices descending (1,3,4,2 for {1,2,3,4} → 23); for a cycle, v0 then odd indices ascending then even indices descending (1,2,4,6,5,3 → 82).
k: Components are paths (m = sz−1) or cycles (m = sz); assign value blocks largest-component-first, cycles before paths of the same size.
Path layout: sorted values in order idx 0,2,4,… then odd idx descending.
Cycle layout: idx 0, then odd idx ascending, then even idx descending.

a.i: Find components via DFS, record size and whether it is a cycle, sort by (size desc, cycle first), carve values n, n−1, … into blocks, lay each block out with the zigzag pattern, and sum adjacent products.
s: Build adjacency; DFS for components, computing size and edge count.
Sort components by size descending, cycles first.
Give each component the next block of largest values, sorted ascending.
Arrange per the path/cycle pattern and sum edge products.
a.t: O(n log n) — component finding is linear, sorting blocks and components dominates

w: Two structural facts do all the work: the graph decomposes into paths/cycles, and big values belong to big components with the zigzag internal order (extremes 1 and 2 land at the ends where they touch fewest products). Validate layouts on the two provided examples before trusting index arithmetic. Pitfall: misclassifying a component as a cycle when m ≠ sz, and 64-bit accumulation for products up to 2.5·10⁹ each. Follow-up: minimize the score instead, or handle disconnected graphs with isolated vertices.
